title: Why does a caterpillar turn into a butterfly instead of just growing bigger?
summary: Watching a caterpillar on a nettle leaf, Maya asks why it has to go through the strange, costly process of becoming a chrysalis at all. The conversation unpicks the idea that a caterpillar and a butterfly are two completely different tools for two completely different jobs — and that the transformation, strange as it is, is one of the most successful inventions in the history of life.
setting: A garden in late summer. A clump of stinging nettles has a cluster of small tortoiseshell caterpillars feeding on the leaves.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: Grandad, why does a caterpillar have to turn into a butterfly? Why doesn't it just grow wings and get bigger?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: What do you think that caterpillar is doing, right now?

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: Eating. It's absolutely destroying that nettle leaf.

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: It really is. Eating is basically all a caterpillar does. What about a butterfly — have you ever seen a butterfly stop and eat a leaf?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: So the caterpillar eats leaves and the butterfly drinks nectar. They're not the same creature doing the same job in different sizes — they're two completely different tools. One is a leaf-eating machine. The other is a flying, flower-visiting, egg-laying machine.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: But why can't it just... do both? Eat leaves AND fly?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: Think about the caterpillar's body — all those legs gripping the leaf, the soft squashy shape. Now think about what a butterfly needs — huge wings, completely different legs, a long coiled tongue for reaching into flowers. They're so different that you can't just add wings to a caterpillar. The whole body plan has to be rebuilt.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: Rebuilt? Is that what happens inside the chrysalis?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: Something extraordinary. When a caterpillar seals itself inside, most of its body actually dissolves — breaks down into a kind of living soup. And then, from that soup, the butterfly is built. New eyes, new legs, wings folded and folded until they fit — all from the same material.

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: If you could ask it, I expect it wouldn't feel like anything. But yes — it really does happen. The tissues break apart, and the butterfly is assembled from the pieces. Some things survive — parts of the nervous system, so the butterfly seems to remember things the caterpillar learned.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: That's so strange. Why go to all that trouble?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: Because it works brilliantly, Maya. The caterpillar doesn't compete with the butterfly. They eat different things, live in different places, need different conditions. One creature gets to have two completely different lives — a feeding life and a flying life. It's been happening for hundreds of millions of years.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: Are these ones going to make a chrysalis soon?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: These are small tortoiseshells — see the orange and black? Their caterpillars will feed for a few more weeks on this nettle patch, then each one will wander off alone and find a quiet spot to hang. You might find a chrysalis under a fence rail or in the shed. Gold-flecked, pointed at the top. Keep an eye out.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: And the butterfly will just... come out of it?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: It'll push its way out, pump blood into its crumpled wings until they expand, and then sit in the sun to dry. And it will never go back to eating nettles. That part of its life is done.

the_heart_of_it: Complete metamorphosis (holometabolism) — the larva/pupa/adult lifecycle — is a key evolutionary innovation found in butterflies and moths, beetles, flies, and many other insects. The caterpillar (larva) is specialised for growth and feeding; the adult is specialised for reproduction and dispersal. The chrysalis (pupa) is the transformation stage, during which larval tissues are histolysed (broken down) and adult structures (imaginal discs, present since the egg) differentiate and develop. The small tortoiseshell (Aglais urticae) is a familiar British garden butterfly whose larvae feed communally on stinging nettles. Research has shown that some learned associations from the larval stage persist through metamorphosis into the adult — though the mechanisms are not fully understood.
watch_for: Saying the caterpillar 'fully dissolves into liquid' is an accessible simplification — what actually happens is that most larval muscles and non-essential tissues are broken down (histolysis), while imaginal discs (clusters of undifferentiated cells present from the beginning) develop into adult structures. The brain and some nervous tissue are largely preserved. Do not say the caterpillar 'dies' inside the chrysalis — it does not; the pupal stage is a living, metabolically active process. The chrysalis is not the same as a cocoon (which is a silk case spun by moth larvae such as silk moths; butterfly pupae are naked chrysalises).
extend_it: Rear a small tortoiseshell from egg to butterfly on cut nettles in a mesh sleeve — watch the instars (the caterpillar shedding its skin as it grows) before the chrysalis stage.
Compare with a grasshopper or a dragonfly — these have incomplete metamorphosis (egg → nymph → adult), no chrysalis stage.
Find a small tortoiseshell chrysalis: it is pale gold-flecked, hung from a pad of silk. Time how long it takes to eclose (emerge) from when it turns transparent.
Look up 'imaginal discs' — the blueprint for the butterfly is present inside the egg from the very start.
